title: Long-Term Redetachment Rates of Pneumatic Retinopexy versus Pars Plana Vitrectomy in Retinal Detachment: A PIVOT Post Hoc Analysis
article_subtype: Post hoc analysis of a randomized trial extension study
condition_or_topic: Long-term retinal redetachment after repair of primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD)
clinical_background: Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) is the most commonly used surgical treatment for primary RRD. The earlier PIVOT trial suggested that pneumatic retinopexy (PnR) should be considered a first-line option for patients meeting its eligibility criteria because it produced better functional outcomes and less morbidity than PPV. PnR uses a gas bubble to temporarily close a retinal break, followed by cryotherapy or laser photocoagulation to create a lasting adhesion; unlike PPV, it does not remove vitreous traction. PIVOT reported reattachment outcomes through 1 year, but longer-term outcomes remained uncertain. Earlier, separate studies reported new retinal tears in 9.7% of patients after a follow-up of 5.5 years without establishing whether these caused redetachment, and redetachment in 6% of patients followed for 7 years after successful reattachment at 12 months.
objectives: Assess long-term redetachment rates after PnR and PPV among PIVOT participants with a minimum follow-up of 2 years.
clinical_question: Among PIVOT participants treated for primary RRD who had no retinal reattachment reintervention within 1 year of the initial procedure and had a minimum follow-up of 2 years (Patient), how does PnR (Intervention) compare with PPV (Comparator) in long-term redetachment rates (Outcome)?
study_design: Post hoc analysis of the PIVOT randomized clinical trial and its long-term extension. The original trial enrolled patients referred between January 2012 and January 2017.

population.description: Patients with primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment who participated in PIVOT. The original trial recruited 176 participants, with 88 in each treatment arm. This analysis included 61 participants treated with PPV and 62 treated with PnR.
inclusion_criteria: Participation in PIVOT with a minimum follow-up of 2 years.
No procedure to reattach the retina within 1 year after the initial study procedure.
exclusion_criteria: A procedure to reattach the retina within the first year after the initial study procedure.
Inability to reach a participant by telephone when documented follow-up was <2 years.
population.mean_age: 68.4 7.74 years in the PPV group; 69.3 9.74 years in the PnR group.
population.care_setting: Department of Ophthalmology, St. Michael’s Hospital, Unity Health Toronto, Toronto, Canada.

interventions: PnR for repair of primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
comparators: PPV for repair of primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

primary: Long-term retinal redetachment rates after PnR compared with PPV.

statistical_methods: Analyses used Jamovi for MacOS version 2.0.0 and SPSS statistics 19 for Windows. Normally distributed continuous variables were summarized as mean and standard deviation; nonnormally distributed variables as median and interquartile range. Categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages. Statistical significance was assessed with a 2-tailed t test and an a of 0.05.
follow_up: Eligibility required at least 2 years of follow-up. Mean follow-up was 5.43 3.60 years in the PPV group and 5.51 3.03 years in the PnR group. Redetachment was assessed through electronic medical records or telephone interviews; telephone contact was required when documented follow-up was <2 years.
interpretation: In this post hoc extension of PIVOT, long-term redetachment was uncommon after both PPV and PnR: 0% and 1.61% (1/62), respectively, without a statistically significant difference (P = 0.32). Mean follow-up was 5.43 3.60 years for PPV and 5.51 3.03 years for PnR. The authors consider both procedures durable options for RRD that rarely require later intervention for redetachment. They conclude that relieving or eliminating vitreous traction with PPV or SB is not necessarily needed for lasting reattachment in most RRDs.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier PnR studies concentrated on the postoperative period, when redetachment risk was greatest: cited estimates were 13% to 17% during the first 3 months and around 10% during the first year. In a retrospective series of 289 patients, 76% of redetachments occurred in the first 4 weeks. For later outcomes, Lisle et al reported 6% redetachment over up to 7 years among eyes attached at 12 months, while Tornambe reported 1% beyond 12 months for both PnR and SB. The authors suggest that procedural differences, including peripheral retinopexy, and pretreatment of lattice and holes in attached retina and strict follow-up in PIVOT may help explain variation between reports. Other cited, nonrandomized studies reported 3.9% long-term redetachment after SB or PPV, alone or combined, 7.1% within 30 months after PPV, and 5.7% within 4 years after SB; these rates exceed that observed in this study’s PPV group. The authors caution that case selection, detachment complexity and risks of postoperative complications affect comparisons with those studies.
clinical_implications: The low late redetachment rate after PnR suggests that adhesion around a retinal break can remain effective despite persistent vitreous traction; the authors do not consider removal of that traction necessary for long-term reattachment in most RRDs.

The authors cite prior evidence associating PnR, compared with PPV, with better visual acuity, less vertical metamorphopsia and aniseikonia, lower morbidity, and better mental-health and vision-related functioning scores. They also cite less frequent and less severe retinal displacement after PnR.
The authors cite studies reporting less cataract formation and subsequent surgery with PnR than with PPV or SB, as well as estimated cost savings of 50.9% versus SB and 59.4% versus PPV.
practice_implications: For primary RRD meeting the PIVOT eligibility criteria, the authors state that PnR should be considered as a first-line treatment, citing its functional outcomes and lower morbidity relative to PPV.
limitations: Not all original PIVOT participants could be included because some were unreachable; consequently, the analysis may have missed some redetachments.
strengths: The underlying PIVOT study was a prospective randomized trial with rigorous inclusion and exclusion criteria.
open_questions: The authors question how many retinal breaks reported after PnR are genuinely new rather than breaks missed initially; they suggest that missed breaks may be underestimated.
main_conclusion: In this long-term PIVOT analysis, redetachment was uncommon after both PnR and PPV, with no statistically significant difference between groups. The authors conclude that both are durable options for RRD and that relieving vitreous traction is not necessarily required for long-term reattachment in most RRDs.
narrative_summary: This post hoc analysis of the PIVOT randomized trial examined redetachment after PnR or PPV for primary RRD. Participants were eligible if they had at least 2 years of follow-up and had not required retinal reattachment intervention during the first year after their initial procedure. Outcomes were assessed through medical records or telephone interviews, according to the available follow-up. Of the original 88 participants in each arm, 61 in the PPV group and 62 in the PnR group were included. Mean follow-up was reported as 5.43 3.60 years for PPV and 5.51 3.03 years for PnR. Long-term redetachment occurred in 0% of the PPV group and 1.61% (1/62) of the PnR group; the difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.32). The sole PnR-group recurrence occurred 6 years after the initial procedure, following a subsequent PPV for symptomatic floaters. The authors interpret the low rates as evidence of durable reattachment with either approach and conclude that vitreous traction need not necessarily be relieved or eliminated to maintain attachment in most RRDs. They caution that some participants could not be reached, so additional redetachments may have been missed.

main_findings.description: Long-term retinal redetachment was uncommon after both PPV and PnR, with no statistically significant difference between groups.
main_findings.context: The analysis included participants who had not undergone a retinal reattachment reintervention during the first year after their initial procedure.

main_findings.description: The participant with recurrent RRD in the PnR group developed photopsia and a visual field defect in the left eye after undergoing PPV for symptomatic floaters following initially successful PnR. The macula remained attached.
main_findings.context: The participant was a 68-year-old man; symptoms occurred 6 years after the initial procedure, and the retina redetached after the subsequent PPV.

secondary_results: The original PIVOT trial recruited 176 participants, with 88 assigned to PPV and 88 to PnR. In the PPV arm, 4 were ineligible because of reintervention during the first year; 23 of the 84 eligible participants were unreachable, leaving 72.6% (61/84) in this analysis.
In the PnR arm, 11 participants were ineligible: 9 underwent reintervention and 2 withdrew. Of the 77 eligible participants, 15 were unreachable, leaving 62 (80.5%) in this analysis.

Among the 61 included PPV participants, redetachment status was assessed by electronic medical chart review for 59.0% (36/61) and by telephone for 41.0% (25/61). Among the 62 included PnR participants, the corresponding figures were 51.2% (32/62) and 48.4% (30/62).
Mean age was 68.4 7.74 years in the PPV group and 69.3 9.74 years in the PnR group. Mean follow-up was 5.43 3.60 years for PPV and 5.51 3.03 years for PnR.
Consecutive visits for 4 years after the initial procedure were recorded for 52.5% (32/61) of included PPV participants and 54.8% (34/62) of included PnR participants.

A previously published retrospective study reported that, among 57 patients with retinal reattachment 1 month after a single PnR operation, 9.7% developed new retinal tears over 5.5 years; it did not establish whether those tears caused another detachment.

A previously published nonrandomized prospective study followed 29 patients whose retinas remained attached at 12 months after PnR. Over 7 years, redetachment occurred in 6% of cases, more than 2.5 years after the initial procedure.

The article cites earlier reports placing redetachment risk after PnR at 13% to 17% during the first 3 months and around 10% during the first year. In a cited retrospective study of 289 patients, 76% of redetachments occurred within the first 4 weeks.

The article reports that Freyler and Radax found significantly more new breaks during the first 3 months, with occurrence decreasing to around 6% in the first 5 years after successful PnR reattachment at 12 months. It describes published estimates of new-break risk as ranging from 7% to 22%.

In previously published longer-term findings, Lisle et al reported redetachment in 6% of patients by 7 years after successful PnR reattachment at 12 months. Tornambe reported redetachment rates of 1% beyond 12 months for both PnR and SB.

A cited retrospective analysis of 155 eyes with mean follow-up of >5 years reported a 3.9% long-term redetachment rate for SB and PPV cases, whether combined or not; 3.2% of eyes contained silicone oil at the final examination.

A cited prospective PPV study reported redetachment in 7.1% within 30 months, with every redetachment occurring in the first 3 months, and a final anatomical reattachment rate of 98.6% after reintervention. A separate retrospective review of phakic eyes treated with SB reported redetachment in 5.7% within 4 years.
Cited economic estimates suggest that PnR costs 50.9% less than SB and 59.4% less than PPV.

document_sections.heading: Purpose
document_sections.content: The study assessed long-term retinal redetachment after pneumatic retinopexy and pars plana vitrectomy among participants in PIVOT.

document_sections.heading: Design
document_sections.content: The authors describe PIVOT as a randomized controlled trial; this study is a post hoc analysis of its long-term extension.

document_sections.heading: Subjects
document_sections.content: The study considered participants from the PIVOT trial.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: At St. Michael’s Hospital, Unity Health Toronto, Toronto, Canada, investigators assessed PIVOT participants treated with PnR or PPV for RRD who had at least 2 years of follow-up. Redetachment was assessed through medical records or telephone interviews; telephone contact was required when documented follow-up was <2 years. Participants were eligible only if they had not undergone another intervention to reattach the retina during the first year after their initial procedure.

document_sections.heading: Main Outcome Measures
document_sections.content: The principal measure was the long-term redetachment rate after RRD repair with PnR compared with PPV.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The analysis included 61 PPV participants and 62 PnR participants. Long-term redetachment occurred in 0% of the PPV group and 1.61% (1/62) of the PnR group (P = 0.32). Mean follow-up, in years, was 5.43 3.60 for PPV versus 5.51 3.03 for PnR.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The long-term redetachment rates did not differ statistically between PnR and PPV. Both remained durable options for RRD over extended follow-up, with additional treatment for redetachment rarely needed.

PPV is the most commonly used surgical treatment for primary RRD. The PIVOT trial suggested considering PnR as first-line treatment when its specific eligibility criteria are met because it yielded better functional outcomes and less morbidity than PPV. PnR places an expansile intravitreal gas bubble, such as sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) or perfluoropropane (C3F8), against a retinal break while the patient maintains a specified head position. Temporary closure limits further fluid entry and permits the retinal pigment epithelial pump to absorb subretinal fluid; cryotherapy or laser photocoagulation then produces an adhesion that seals the break. Although PIVOT reported reattachment through 1 year, longer-term outcomes remained uncertain because PnR does not address vitreous traction, an important factor in RRD. In a retrospective study published in 1993, 57 patients had achieved reattachment 1 month after a single PnR operation; 9.7% developed new tears over 5.5 years of follow-up. That study did not establish whether those tears caused another detachment or how many patients attached at 1 year detached later. A nonrandomized prospective study published in 1998 followed 29 patients for 7 years after successful reattachment at 12 months with one PnR intervention for primary RRD; redetachment occurred in 6% of cases >2.5 years after the initial procedure. Limited long-term evidence has sustained debate about PnR durability, including concern that detachment may recur years later. The present study aimed to compare long-term redetachment after PnR and PPV among PIVOT participants followed for at least 2 years; PIVOT was a prospective randomized trial with rigorous eligibility criteria.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: This post hoc analysis used PIVOT randomized-trial data from patients with primary RRD referred to the Department of Ophthalmology at St. Michael’s Hospital, Toronto, Canada, between January 2012 and January 2017. An ethics committee approved the work, participants gave informed consent, and the study followed the Declaration of Helsinki. Most patients remained under the care of their original retinal surgeon after the trial’s first year and entered the long-term extension. Participants were excluded if they needed retinal reattachment intervention within 1 year of their original study procedure, since those outcomes had already been reported; inclusion also required at least 2 years of follow-up. Investigators determined redetachment from electronic records or direct telephone interviews and recorded the interval from presentation to the last documented follow-up. For >6 years of documented follow-up, records alone were used. For 2 to 5 years, records were reviewed before a call about later reintervention. With <2 years of documented follow-up, telephone contact was mandatory; patients who could not be reached were excluded. During calls, participants were asked about detachment in the study eye since their last recorded visit, any subsequent operating-theater visit concerning that eye, scheduled procedures for it, and eye-specific comments or concerns.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analyses
document_sections.content: Analyses used Jamovi for MacOS version 2.0.0 and SPSS statistics 19 for Windows. Normally distributed continuous data were expressed as mean and standard deviation, and nonnormally distributed continuous data as median and interquartile range. Categorical data were given as counts and percentages. Statistical significance was assessed with a 2-tailed t test and an a of 0.05.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: PIVOT recruited 176 patients, with 88 in each of the PPV and PnR arms. In the PPV arm, 4 were ineligible after first-year reintervention. In the PnR arm, 11 were ineligible: 9 had reinterventions and 2 withdrew. Among 84 eligible PPV participants, 23 could not be reached, leaving 72.6% (61/84) for analysis. Of those included, 59.0% (36/61) were assessed through electronic records and 41.0% (25/61) through telephone calls. Among 77 eligible PnR participants, 15 could not be reached; 62 (80.5%) were included. Their assessments used records for 51.2% (32/62) and calls for 48.4% (30/62). Mean age was 68.4 7.74 years in the PPV group and 69.3 9.74 years in the PnR group. Mean follow-up, in years, was 5.43 3.60 for PPV versus 5.51 3.03 for PnR. Consecutive visits for 4 years after the initial procedure were documented for 52.5% (32/61) of the PPV group and 54.8% (34/62) of the PnR group. Combining records and calls, long-term redetachment was 0% with PPV and 1.61% (1/62) with PnR, without a statistically significant between-group difference (P = 0.32). The sole PnR participant with recurrent RRD was a 68-year-old man who developed photopsia and a visual-field defect 6 years after the initial procedure in his left eye. After successful PnR, he had undergone PPV for symptomatic floaters, followed by redetachment. His macula remained attached, and final visual acuity was 20/30. Figure 1 summarizes participant inclusion and whether redetachment was determined by record review or telephone interview; Figure 2 summarizes descriptive statistics for both treatment groups.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: In this PIVOT extension post hoc analysis, redetachment assessed on average 4.5 years after primary RRD was very uncommon and similar across groups: 0% after PPV and 1.61% after PnR. The authors interpret both procedures as durable, while noting that long-term evidence for PnR in primary RRD has been limited. Earlier PnR studies mainly evaluated the first 6 months, when detachment risk is highest. Cited studies reported risks of 13% to 17% within the first 3 months and around 10% within the first year; risk was greater nearer the procedure. In a retrospective series of 289 patients, 76% of redetachments occurred in the first 4 weeks after PnR. Mudvari et al attributed early redetachment mainly to new breaks. Freyler and Radax found significantly more new breaks during the first 3 months, with occurrence declining to around 6% in the first 5 years among patients successfully attached with PnR at 12 months. Reported new-break risks range from 7% to 22%, but the authors question whether some breaks were initially missed. They suggest missed breaks could contribute to early redetachment and may be undercounted. Longer-follow-up studies appear to report lower redetachment rates: among patients attached at 12 months after PnR, Lisle et al found 6% through 7 years, while Tornambe reported 1% beyond 12 months for both PnR and SB. Technique may explain some variation. Across 310 eyes treated with PnR over 10 years, Tornambe found that complete peripheral retinopexy significantly affected success. The authors suggest that PIVOT technique might have contributed to their low long-term PnR rate, also described as 1.6%. A retrospective analysis of 155 eyes with mean follow-up >5 years reported 3.9% long-term redetachment after SB and PPV, alone or combined; 3.2% of eyes still contained silicone oil at the final examination. A prospective PPV study reported 7.1% redetachment over 30 months, all within the first 3 months, and 98.6% final anatomic reattachment after reintervention. A retrospective review of phakic eyes treated with SB for primary RRD found 5.7% redetachment within 4 years. Those rates exceed the present PPV-group rate, but they came from nonrandomized data outside a trial. The authors note that selection bias affects outcomes because detachments vary in complexity and in risk factors for proliferative vitreoretinopathy and other postoperative complications. They propose that treating lattice and holes in attached retina before PnR, together with strict follow-up schedules, might help explain differences from retrospective reports; these practices were not described in older studies. Another limitation is that unreachable PIVOT participants could not all be included, so some redetachments might have been missed. Considered alongside earlier work, the findings suggest low long-term redetachment after PnR, comparable to other surgical approaches. Regarding vitreous traction, SB uses a silicone exoplant for lasting scleral indentation around causative tears and changes vitreous-current dynamics; PPV reduces traction by removing vitreous. PnR instead forms a laser- or cryopexy-induced chorioretinal adhesion capable of resisting traction without removing it. The authors describe its use even for RRD involving multiple tears, retinal dialysis, or large or giant breaks. They suggest laser retinopexy can maintain adhesion around a break despite ongoing traction. Treated horseshoe tears without detachment provide another example: most do not subsequently detach, suggesting that laser alone can overcome traction and that traction removal or an SB is probably unnecessary in most such cases. The authors identify minimal invasiveness and functional recovery as principal reasons to choose PnR over PPV. Cited comparisons associate PnR with better visual acuity, less vertical metamorphopsia and aniseikonia, less morbidity, and higher mental-health and vision-related-function scores; retinal displacement is more frequent and severe after PPV. Studies comparing PnR separately with PPV and SB found substantially less cataract formation and subsequent surgery with PnR. The authors also report superior functional outcomes and vision-related quality of life during the first 6 months, alongside greater cost-effectiveness: estimated savings are 50.9% versus SB and 59.4% versus PPV. Accounting for the greater proportion of PPV-treated eyes requiring later cataract extraction would increase estimated savings. In cited work, eyes needing another procedure after failed PnR had anatomic and functional outcomes comparable to eyes reattached initially. The authors therefore regard first-line PnR as advantageous in the long term for patients and the health care system.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: This post hoc analysis of the long-term PIVOT extension found very low redetachment rates after both PnR and PPV, with no statistically significant difference. Follow-up was 5.43 3.60 years after PPV and 5.51 3.03 years after PnR. Both approaches remained durable RRD treatments over extended follow-up and seldom required additional redetachment intervention. The authors conclude that relieving or eliminating vitreous traction with PPV or SB is not necessarily needed for long-term reattachment in most RRDs.
